Kipchoge: In April, Kipchoge won the [[2016 London Marathon]] for the second consecutive year in a time of 2:03:05.<ref>{{Cite web |url=https://bleacherreport.com/articles/2635264-london-marathon-2016-results-men-and-womens-top-finishers |title=Retrieved 22 May 2016. |website=[[Bleacher Report]] |access-date=22 May 2016 |archive-date=5 June 2016 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20160605011107/http://bleacherreport.com/articles/2635264-london-marathon-2016-results-men-and-womens-top-finishers |url-status=live }}</ref> His performance broke the course record in London and became the second-fastest marathon time in history, missing [[Dennis Kimetto]]'s world record by 8 seconds.<ref>{{Cite web |url=https://www.iaaf.org/records/all-time-toplists/road-running/marathon/outdoor/men/senior?regionType=world&drop=regular&fiftyPercentRule=regular&page=1&bestResultsOnly=true&firstDay=1899-12-31&lastDay=2016-04-24 |title=Retrieved 20 September 2018. |access-date=20 September 2018 |archive-date=20 September 2018 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20180920122639/https://www.iaaf.org/records/all-time-toplists/road-running/marathon/outdoor/men/senior?regionType=world&drop=regular&fiftyPercentRule=regular&page=1&bestResultsOnly=true&firstDay=1899-12-31&lastDay=2016-04-24 |url-status=live }}</ref>
Kipchoge: As the prerace favourite, during the [[Athletics at the 2016 Summer Olympics|2016 Rio Summer Olympics]], Kipchoge gained a gold medal in the [[athletics at the 2016 Summer Olympics|marathon]] event.<ref>{{Cite news |url=https://www.runnersworld.com/news/a20818616/mens-marathon-eliud-kipchoge-wins-galen-rupp-gets-bronze/ |title=Men's Marathon: Eliud Kipchoge Wins, Galen Rupp Gets Bronze |date=21 August 2016 |work=Runner's World |access-date=4 October 2018 |language=en-US |archive-date=4 October 2018 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20181004230031/https://www.runnersworld.com/news/a20818616/mens-marathon-eliud-kipchoge-wins-galen-rupp-gets-bronze/ |url-status=live }}</ref><ref>{{Cite news |url=https://www.bbc.com/sport/olympics/36727865 |title=Rio Olympics 2016: Kenya's Eliud Kipchoge wins men's marathon |date=21 August 2016 |work=BBC Sport |access-date=26 September 2018 |language=en-GB |archive-date=26 September 2018 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20180926212641/https://www.bbc.com/sport/olympics/36727865 |url-status=live }}</ref><ref>{{Cite web |url=http://www.latimes.com/sports/olympics/la-sp-oly-rio-2016-kipchoge-of-kenya-wins-men-s-marathon-1471791537-htmlstory.html |title=Rio Olympics: Eliud Kipchoge of Kenya wins men's marathon; Galen Rupp of the U.S. takes bronze |last=Dillman |first=Lisa |website=[[Los Angeles Times]] |date=27 August 2016 |access-date=26 September 2018 |archive-date=26 September 2018 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20180926205804/http://www.latimes.com/sports/olympics/la-sp-oly-rio-2016-kipchoge-of-kenya-wins-men-s-marathon-1471791537-htmlstory.html |url-status=live }}</ref> On the last day of the Olympic Games on 21 August 2016, he won in a time of 2:08:44. The runner up was Feyisa Lilesa (Ethiopia) in 2:09:54 and the bronze medal went to Galen Rupp (USA), doing his second marathon, crossing the finish line in 2:10:05. When the halfway point after 21.0975 km was reached, 37 men were within 10 seconds of the lead runner. The participants' field diminished to 3 lead runners shortly before 34 km. Kipchoge made his final move on silver medal winner Lilesa around 36 km into the race. He covered the first half of the race in 1:05:55 while doing the second half in 1:02:49, which amounts to a difference of more than 3 minutes, a negative split.<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://www.iaaf.org/news/report/rio-2016-men-marathon|title=IAAF: Report: men's marathon – Rio 2016 Olympic Games{{!}} News {{!}} iaaf.org|website=iaaf.org|access-date=29 September 2018|archive-date=16 September 2018|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20180916160144/https://www.iaaf.org/news/report/rio-2016-men-marathon|url-status=live}}</ref><ref name="Ingle">{{Cite web |url=https://www.theguardian.com/sport/2016/aug/21/eliud-kipchoge-callum-hawkins-feyisa-lilesa-olympic-marathon |title=Eliud Kipchoge powers to marathon gold as Callum Hawkins finishes ninth |last=Ingle |first=Sean |date=21 August 2016 |website=The Guardian |language=en |access-date=28 September 2018 |archive-date=21 August 2016 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20160821222328/https://www.theguardian.com/sport/2016/aug/21/eliud-kipchoge-callum-hawkins-feyisa-lilesa-olympic-marathon |url-status=live }}</ref> The winning gap between Kipchoge and Lilesa by 70 seconds was the largest victory margin since the [[Athletics at the 1972 Summer Olympics – Men's marathon|1972 Olympic marathon]].<ref>{{Cite news |url=https://www.flotrack.org/articles/5054839-eliud-kipchoge-wins-olympic-marathon-galen-rupp-takes-bronze |title=Eliud Kipchoge Wins Olympic Marathon, Galen Rupp Takes Bronze |access-date=28 September 2018 |language=en-US |archive-date=29 September 2018 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20180929000314/https://www.flotrack.org/articles/5054839-eliud-kipchoge-wins-olympic-marathon-galen-rupp-takes-bronze |url-status=live }}</ref> Kipchoge's winning time of 2:08:44 was, as of August 2021, his slowest marathon time. One hundred fifty-five runners started the race, the largest field in Olympic history; 140 of them finished the race.<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://www.iaaf.org/competitions/olympic-games/the-xxxi-olympic-games-5771/results/men/marathon/final/result|title=IAAF: Marathon Result {{!}} The XXXI Olympic Games {{!}} iaaf.org|website=iaaf.org|access-date=29 September 2018|archive-date=29 September 2018|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20180929233451/https://www.iaaf.org/competitions/olympic-games/the-xxxi-olympic-games-5771/results/men/marathon/final/result|url-status=live}}</ref><ref>{{Cite news |url=http://www.espn.com/espnw/sports/article/17359189/eliud-kipchoge-kenya-wins-olympic-men-marathon-american-galen-rupp-takes-bronze |title=Eliud Kipchoge of Kenya wins Olympic men's marathon; American Galen Rupp takes bronze |work=espnW |access-date=28 September 2018 |archive-date=29 September 2018 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20180929000531/http://www.espn.com/espnw/sports/article/17359189/eliud-kipchoge-kenya-wins-olympic-men-marathon-american-galen-rupp-takes-bronze |url-status=live }}</ref> With this win, Kipchoge became the second Kenyan male after Sammy Wanjiru in [[Athletics at the 2008 Summer Olympics|Beijing 2008]] to win an Olympic marathon gold medal. At the same Olympics, the women's marathon was won by [[Jemima Sumgong]], who became the first female Kenyan winner.<ref>{{Cite web |url=https://www.theguardian.com/sport/2016/aug/14/jemima-sumgong-wins-olympic-marathon-gold-kenya |title=Jemima Sumgong wins Olympic marathon gold for Kenya |author=<!--not stated--> |agency=Reuters |date=14 August 2016 |website=The Guardian |language=en |access-date=1 October 2018 |archive-date=2 October 2018 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20181002020158/https://www.theguardian.com/sport/2016/aug/14/jemima-sumgong-wins-olympic-marathon-gold-kenya |url-status=live }}</ref><ref name="Ingle" />
Kipchoge: On 6 May, Kipchoge, along with Zersenay Tadese (then world record holder in the half marathon) and [[Lelisa Desisa]] (2-time Boston Marathon winner), attempted the first sub-two-hour assisted marathon in the Nike [[Breaking2]] project on the [[Monza]] [[Autodromo Nazionale Monza|Formula 1 racetrack]] near [[Milan]], Italy. All three runners ran a test 2 months before the attempt. The target time was 1 hour for a half Marathon. Kipchoge finished first in 59:17. The course was measured at 2400 m per lap.<ref>{{Cite web |url=https://www.runnersworld.com/news/a20849569/sub-2-marathon-test-run-yields-fast-times-lingering-questions/ |title=Sub-2 Marathon Test Run Yields Fast Times, Lingering Questions |last=Hutchinson |first=Alex |date=7 March 2017 |website=Runner's World |language=en-US |access-date=10 May 2019 |archive-date=10 May 2019 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20190510141834/https://www.runnersworld.com/news/a20849569/sub-2-marathon-test-run-yields-fast-times-lingering-questions/ |url-status=live }}</ref> During the 2-hour attempt, the runners were paced by a lead car and 30 supporting pacers joining in stages (both considered illegal under [[IAAF]] rules).<ref name="veconomist">{{cite news |author=J.S. |title=Can the marathon's two-hour barrier be broken? |url=https://www.economist.com/blogs/gametheory/2017/10/runnin-down-dream |newspaper=[[The Economist]] |date=4 October 2017 |access-date=4 October 2017 |archive-date=15 May 2018 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20180515095632/https://www.economist.com/blogs/gametheory/2017/10/runnin-down-dream |url-status=live }}</ref> The race started at 5:45h local time on the 2.4 km track. Kipchoge finished in 2:00:25, while the other two had to slow and finished far behind.<ref>{{Cite web |url=http://www.herbertsteffny.de/artikel/Nike_Sub_2Hours.htm |title=Sub 2:00 Hours Marathon – kritisch hinterfragt |website=herbertsteffny.de |language=de-de |access-date=29 September 2018 |archive-date=13 October 2018 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20181013041808/http://www.herbertsteffny.de/artikel/Nike_Sub_2Hours.htm |url-status=live }}</ref> The runners planned even 14:13 5k splits to break 2 hours. His 5k splits were: 14:14, 14:07, 14:13, 14:15, 14:14, 14:17, 14:17, 14:27, and 6:20 to finish.<ref>{{Cite news |url=https://www.theguardian.com/sport/live/2017/may/06/sub-two-hour-marathon-attempt-in-monza-live |title=Eliud Kipchoge misses sub two-hour marathon target in Monza – as it happened |last=Caroll |first=James |date=6 May 2017 |work=The Guardian |access-date=30 April 2018 |language=en-GB |issn=0261-3077 |archive-date=22 April 2018 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20180422224117/https://www.theguardian.com/sport/live/2017/may/06/sub-two-hour-marathon-attempt-in-monza-live |url-status=live }}</ref> The 5k split times from 25k and further would be world records: 25k in 1:11:03, 30k in 1:25:20, 35k in 1:39:37, 40k in 1:54:04.
Kipchoge: On 24 September, he won the [[2017 Berlin Marathon]] in a time of 2:03:32.<ref>{{Cite news |url=https://www.bmw-berlin-marathon.com/en/news-and-media/news/2017/09/24/eliud-kipchoge-wins-dramatic-race-in-berlin-with-world-leading-time.html |title=BMW BERLIN-MARATHON |access-date=30 April 2018 |archive-date=15 September 2018 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20180915121103/https://www.bmw-berlin-marathon.com/en/news-and-media/news/2017/09/24/eliud-kipchoge-wins-dramatic-race-in-berlin-with-world-leading-time.html |url-status=live }}</ref> In rainy conditions, he finished 14 seconds ahead of [[Guye Adola]] who ran his first marathon, and set the fastest marathon debut ever.<ref>{{Cite news |url=http://www.bz-berlin.de/berlin/44-berlin-marathon-eliud-kipchoge-ergebnis-zeit-weltrekord |title=44. Kipchoge: On 16 September, Kipchoge won the [[2018 Berlin Marathon]] in a time of 2:01:39, breaking the previous world record by 1 minute and 18 seconds (2:02:57 set by fellow countryman Dennis Kimetto at the Berlin Marathon in 2014). It was the greatest improvement in a marathon world record time since 1967.<ref>{{cite web |last1=Robinson |first1=Roger |title=Eliud Kipchoge Crushes Marathon World Record at Berlin Marathon |date=16 September 2018 |url=https://www.runnersworld.com/news/a23244541/berlin-marathon-world-record/ |publisher=Runner's World |access-date=21 October 2019 |archive-date=31 August 2019 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20190831110153/https://www.runnersworld.com/news/a23244541/berlin-marathon-world-record/ |url-status=live }}</ref> He finished 4:43 min ahead of second-placed fellow Kenyan Amos Kipruto. The world record holder from 2013, Wilson Kipsang of Kenya, came in third at 2:06:48.<ref>{{Cite news |url=https://www.welt.de/sport/article181548434/Berlin-Marathon-2018-Kenianer-Eliud-Kipchoge-knackt-den-Weltrekord.html |title=Berlin-Marathon 2018: Kenianer Eliud Kipchoge knackt den Weltrekord |last=WELT |date=16 September 2018 |work=DIE WELT |language=de |access-date=16 September 2018 |archive-date=19 September 2018 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20180919100330/https://www.welt.de/sport/article181548434/Berlin-Marathon-2018-Kenianer-Eliud-Kipchoge-knackt-den-Weltrekord.html |url-status=live }}</ref><ref>{{Cite web|url=https://www.iaaf.org/news/report/wilson-kipsang-sets-world-record-of-20323-in|title=IAAF: Kipsang sets world record of 2:03:23 at Berlin Marathon|website=iaaf.org|access-date=17 September 2018|archive-date=26 March 2018|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20180326142253/https://www.iaaf.org/news/report/wilson-kipsang-sets-world-record-of-20323-in|url-status=live}}</ref> It was the 11th world record set at the Berlin Marathon.<ref name="BerlinRecords" />

Kipchoge: Kipchoge successfully defended his title from the Rio Olympics by winning the gold medal in the men's marathon at the Tokyo Games in a time of 2:08:38, becoming only the third person to successfully defend their gold medal in the men's marathon, after [[Abebe Bikila]] in 1960 and 1964, and [[Waldemar Cierpinski]] in 1976 and 1980.<ref>{{Cite news|last=Longman|first=Jeré|date=8 August 2021|title=Kipchoge finished far ahead of the pack to defend his men's Olympic marathon title.|language=en-US|work=The New York Times|url=https://www.nytimes.com/2021/08/07/sports/olympics/marathon-results-kipchoge-galen-rupp.html|access-date=8 August 2021|issn=0362-4331|archive-date=8 August 2021|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20210808010742/https://www.nytimes.com/2021/08/07/sports/olympics/marathon-results-kipchoge-galen-rupp.html|url-status=live}}</ref> He was the favourite to win and attacked around the 30 km mark, looking back only once afterwards. He won by 80 seconds, the largest margin in 49 years.<ref>{{Cite web |last= |date=12 January 2022 |title=2021 LetsRun Awards |url=https://www.letsrun.com/news/2022/01/2021-letsrun-awards-best-athlete-best-comeback-best-wtf-performance-biggest-heartbreak-more/ |access-date=3 January 2023 |website=[[LetsRun.com]] |language=en |archive-date=3 January 2023 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20230103132745/https://www.letsrun.com/news/2022/01/2021-letsrun-awards-best-athlete-best-comeback-best-wtf-performance-biggest-heartbreak-more/ |url-status=live }}</ref> The silver medal went to [[Abdi Nageeye]] (Netherlands), while [[Bashir Abdi]] (Belgium) came in third for a bronze medal with 2:10:00. Kipchoge: On 25 September, Kipchoge won the [[2022 Berlin Marathon|Berlin Marathon]] decisively in a time of 2:01:09, beating by 30 seconds his own previous world record, which he set on the same course in 2018. He finished 4:49 min ahead of second-placed compatriot [[Mark Korir]] while Ethiopia's Tadu Abate took third place with a time of 2:06:28. Kipchoge achieved halfway in 59:51 which, being at the time, the fastest split in marathon history, would have been a world record in the standalone half-marathon in 1993, and was only 26 seconds off his best in that distance. It [[Orbital period|completes an orbit]] ([[lunar month]]) in relation to Earth and the [[Sun]] ([[Lunation|synodically]]) every 29.5 days. The Moon and Earth are bound by [[gravitational]] attraction, which is stronger on the sides facing each other. The resulting [[tidal force]]s are the main driver of Earth's [[tide]]s, and have pulled the Moon to always face Earth with the same [[Near side of the Moon|near side]]. This [[tidal locking]] effectively synchronizes the Moon's [[Rotation period (astronomy)|rotation period]] ([[lunar day]]) to its orbital period (lunar month). 75: In [[geophysical definition of planet|geophysical terms]], the Moon is a [[planetary-mass object]] or [[satellite planet]]. Its mass is 1.2% that of the Earth, and its diameter is {{cvt|3474|km|mi}}, roughly one-quarter of Earth's (about as wide as the [[contiguous United States]]). Within the [[Solar System]], it is [[List of Solar System objects by size|larger and more massive]] than any known [[dwarf planet]], and the fifth-largest and fifth–most massive moon, as well as the largest and most massive in relation to its [[primary body|parent planet]]. Its [[surface gravity]] is about one-sixth of Earth's, about half that of [[Mars]], and the second-highest among all moons in the Solar System after [[Jupiter]]'s moon [[Io (moon)|Io]]. The body of the Moon is [[Planetary differentiation|differentiated]] and [[Terrestrial planet|terrestrial]], with only a minuscule [[hydrosphere]], [[Atmosphere of the Moon|atmosphere]], and [[Magnetic field of the Moon|magnetic field]]. The [[lunar surface]] is covered in [[Lunar regolith|regolith dust]], which mainly consists of the fine [[Ejecta blanket|material ejected]] from the [[lunar crust]] by [[impact event]]s. The lunar crust is marked by [[impact crater]]s; some younger ones feature bright [[Ray system|ray-like streaks]]. The Moon was volcanically active until 1.2 billion years ago, surfacing lava mostly on the thinner near side of the Moon, filling ancient craters, which through cooling formed the today prominently visible dark plains of [[basalt]] called [[Lunar mare|maria]] ('seas'). The [[origin of the Moon]] is not clear, although it is thought to have been formed out of material from Earth that was ejected by [[giant-impact hypothesis|a giant impact]] of a [[Theia (planet)|Mars-sized body]] 4.51 billion years ago, not long after [[Age of Earth|Earth's formation]]. 77: From a distance, the day and night phases of the lunar day are visible as the [[lunar phases]], and when the Moon passes through [[Earth's shadow]] a [[lunar eclipse]] is observable. The Moon's [[apparent size]] in Earth's sky is about the same as that of the Sun, which causes it to cover the Sun completely during a total [[solar eclipse]]. The Moon is the [[List of brightest natural objects in the sky|brightest celestial object]] in Earth's [[night sky]] because of its large apparent size, while the [[reflectance]] (albedo) of its surface is comparable to that of [[Asphalt concrete|asphalt]]. About 59% of the surface of the Moon is visible from Earth owing to the different angles at which the Moon can appear in Earth's sky ([[libration]]), making parts of the [[far side of the Moon]] visible. 79: The Moon has been an important source of inspiration and knowledge in human history, having been crucial to [[cosmography]], [[mythology]], [[Lunar deity|religion]], art, [[Lunar calendar|time keeping]], [[natural science]] and [[spaceflight]]. The [[Timeline of Solar System exploration|first spaceflights]] to an extraterrestrial body were to the Moon, starting in 1959 with the [[Flyby (spaceflight)|flyby]] of ''[[Luna 1]]'' (sent by the [[Soviet Union]]), and the [[Impactor (spacecraft)|intentional impact]] of ''[[Luna 2]]'', followed in 1966 by the first [[soft landing]] (by ''[[Luna 9]]'') and [[orbital insertion]] (by ''[[Luna 10]]''). Humans first arrived in orbit with [[Apollo 8]] (sent by the [[United States]]) on December 24, 1968, and then on the surface with [[Apollo 11]] on July 20, 1969, making the Moon the only celestial body beyond Earth that humans have visited. By 1972, six Apollo missions had landed [[List of people who have flown to the Moon#People who walked on the Moon|twelve people]] on the Moon and stayed up to three days. Renewed robotic [[exploration of the Moon]], in particular to confirm the presence of [[Lunar water|water on the Moon]], has fueled plans to return humans to the Moon, starting with the [[Artemis program]] scheduled for the late 2020s. 82: The English proper name for Earth's natural satellite is typically written as ''Moon'', with a capital ''M''.{{cite web |url=http://www.iau.org/public_press/themes/naming/#spelling |title=Naming Astronomical Objects: Spelling of Names |publisher=[[International Astronomical Union]] |access-date=April 6, 2020 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20081216024716/http://www.iau.org/public_press/themes/naming/#spelling |archive-date=December 16, 2008}} The noun ''moon'' is derived from [[Old English]] {{lang|ang|mōna}}, which stems from {{lang|gem-x-proto|mēnōn}},{{cite book |first=Vladimir |last=Orel |year=2003 |url=https://archive.org/details/Orel-AHandbookOfGermanicEtymology/mode/2up/search/moon |title=A Handbook of Germanic Etymology |publisher=Brill |access-date=March 5, 2020}} which in turn comes from [[Proto-Indo-European]] {{lang|ine-x-proto|mēnsis}} ('month'){{cite dictionary |entry=*mēnsis |first=Fernando |last=López-Menchero |url=https://indo-european.info/dictionary-translator/word.inc.php/ine/m%c4%93nsis |dictionary=Late Proto-Indo-European Etymological Lexicon |date=May 22, 2020 |access-date=July 30, 2022 |archive-date=May 22, 2020 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20200522153418/https://indo-european.info/dictionary-translator/word.inc.php/ine/m%c4%93nsis |url-status=live}}{{snd}}from earlier {{lang|ine-x-proto|mēnōt}} (genitive {{lang|ine-x-proto|mēneses}}), which may be related to a verb meaning 'to measure [time]'. 84: The Latin name for the Moon is {{lang|la|lūna}}. The English adjective ''lunar'' was ultimately borrowed from Latin, likely through French. In scientific writing and science fiction, the Moon is sometimes referred to as ''Luna'' {{IPAc-en|'|l|uː|n|ə}}For example: {{cite book |first=James A. |last=Hall III |date=2016 |title=Moons of the Solar System |publisher=Springer |isbn=978-3-319-20636-3}} to distinguish it from other moons. In poetry, ''Luna'' may also refer to the [[personification]] of the Moon as a woman.{{OED|Luna}} 86: The Ancient Greek word {{tlit|grc|selḗnē}} referred to the Moon as a celestial body, and also to the moon goddess [[Selene]] {{IPAc-en|s|ə|ˈ|l|iː|n|iː}}. The rare English adjective ''selenian'' {{IPAc-en|s|ə|l|iː|n|i|ə|n}}{{MW|selenian}} is used to describe the Moon as a world, as opposed to a celestial object.{{OED|selenian}} Its cognate ''selenic'', originally a rare synonym,{{OED|selenic}} now almost always refers to the chemical element [[selenium]].{{MW|selenic}} The corresponding prefix ''seleno-'' appears in terms including ''[[selenography]]'' (the study of the lunar surface).{{LSJ|selh/nh |σελήνη |ref}}. 88: [[Artemis]], the Greek goddess of the wilderness and the hunt, also came to be identified with Selene, and was sometimes called [[Cynthia]] after her birthplace on [[Mount Cynthus]].{{cite book |first=Imke |last=Pannen |title=When the Bad Bleeds: Mantic Elements in English Renaissance Revenge Tragedy |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=37CPbHwqPjwC&pg=PA96 |year=2010 |publisher=V&R |isbn=978-3-89971-640-5 |page=96}} Her Roman equivalent is [[Diana (mythology)|Diana]]. 90: The [[astronomical symbols]] for the Moon are the crescent [[File:Moon crescent symbol (bold).svg|24px|☽|class=skin-invert]] and decrescent [[File:Moon decrescent symbol (bold).svg|24px|☾|class=skin-invert]], for example in ''M''☾ 'lunar mass'. 93: The International Astronomical Union (IAU) calls Earth's satellite "the Moon", with a capital "M".{{Cite web |title=International Astronomical Union {{!}} IAU |url=https://iauarchive.eso.org/public/themes/our_moon/ |access-date=2025-12-31 |website=iauarchive.eso.org}} Other natural satellites of planets are called 'moons', with a lower-case "m".{{Cite web |title=Frequently Asked Questions |url=https://www.iau.org/IAU/Iau/Science/What-we-do/FAQs.aspx |access-date=2025-12-31 |website=www.iau.org}} 94: The Moon has historically been identified as a [[classical planet]], in the original sense of a wandering object in the sky. # Using variable moon_info from context
_ = moon_info

# Calculations:
# Minimum perigee value on the Wikipedia page for the Moon: 356,400 km
# Kipchoge's world record marathon pace:
# Marathon distance: 42.195 km
# Record time: 2:01:09 (2022 Berlin Marathon) = 2*3600 + 1*60 + 9 = 7269 seconds = 2.0191666666666667 hours
# Speed = 42.195 km / (7269 / 3600 h) = 20.897234832851837 km/h

# Total hours to cover minimum perigee distance (356,400 km):
min_perigee_km = 356400
marathon_km = 42.195
time_sec = 2 * 3600 + 1 * 60 + 9 # 2:01:09
speed = marathon_km / (time_sec / 3600)
hours = min_perigee_km / speed
thousand_hours = hours / 1000
nearest_1000_hours = round(hours, -3)

# If using 2018 record (2:01:39 = 7299 s):
speed_2018 = marathon_km / (7299 / 3600)
hours_2018 = min_perigee_km / speed_2018
nearest_1000_2018 = round(hours_2018, -3)

# If using INEOS 1:59:40 (7180 s):
speed_ineos = marathon_km / (7180 / 3600)
hours_ineos = min_perigee_km / speed_ineos
nearest_1000_ineos = round(hours_ineos, -3)

print(f"2022 WR Hours: {hours:.2f}, 1000 hours: {nearest_1000_hours}")
print(f"2018 WR Hours: {hours_2018:.2f}, 1000 hours: {nearest_1000_2018}")
print(f"INEOS Hours: {hours_ineos:.2f}, 1000 hours: {nearest_1000_ineos}")
print(f"Result in thousand hours (e.g. 17 or 17000): {round(thousand_hours)}")

python -c "
    import urllib.request
    import json
    
    # Fetch Moon wikitext
    url = 'https://en.wikipedia.org/w/api.php?action=parse&page=Moon&prop=wikitext&format=json'
    req = urllib.request.Request(url, headers={'User-Agent': 'Mozilla/5.0'})
    res = urllib.request.urlopen(req)
    data = json.loads(res.read().decode('utf-8'))
    wt_moon = data['parse']['wikitext']['*']
    
    for line in wt_moon.splitlines():
        if 'perigee' in line.lower():
            print('Moon perigee:', line)
    
    # Fetch Kipchoge wikitext or world record marathon pace
    url_k = 'https://en.wikipedia.org/w/api.php?action=parse&page=Eliud_Kipchoge&prop=wikitext&format=json'
    req_k = urllib.request.Request(url_k, headers={'User-Agent': 'Mozilla/5.0'})
    res_k = urllib.request.urlopen(req_k)
    data_k = json.loads(res_k.read().decode('utf-8'))
    wt_k = data_k['parse']['wikitext']['*']
    
    for line in wt_k.splitlines():
        if 'marathon' in line.lower() and ('record' in line.lower() or '2:0' in line.lower() or '1:59' in line.lower()):
            print('Kipchoge:', line)
    "

Moon perigee: The Moon's orbit is slightly elliptical, with an [[orbital eccentricity]] of 0.055. The [[semi-major axis]] of the geocentric lunar orbit, called the [[lunar distance]], is approximately {{cvt|385,000|km|mi}}, or 1.3 [[light-second]]s, comparable to going [[circumference of Earth|around Earth]] approximately 9.6 times.{{efn |name=distance ratio}}<ref name="allen">{{cite book |last1=Allen |first1=C. W. |title=Allen's Astrophysical Quantities |date=2002 |publisher=Springer |location=New York |isbn=978-1-4612-1186-0 |edition=4th|pages=240,308}}</ref> The distance between the Moon and Earth varies from around {{convert|356,400|km|mi|abbr=on}} ([[perigee]]) to {{convert|406,700|km|mi|abbr=on}} (apogee), making the Moon's distance and apparent size fluctuate up to 14%.<ref name="size1">{{cite web |author=Phillips |first=Tony |date=March 16, 2011 |title=Super Full Moon |url=https://science.nasa.gov/science-news/science-at-nasa/2011/16mar_supermoon/ |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20120507035348/https://science.nasa.gov/science-news/science-at-nasa/2011/16mar_supermoon/ |archive-date=May 7, 2012 |access-date=March 19, 2011 |publisher=NASA}}</ref><ref name="size2">{{cite news |author=De Atley |first=Richard K. |date=March 18, 2011 |title=Full moon tonight is as close as it gets |url=http://www.pe.com/localnews/stories/PE_News_Local_D_moon19.23a6364.html |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20110322161600/http://www.pe.com/localnews/stories/PE_News_Local_D_moon19.23a6364.html |archive-date=March 22, 2011 |access-date=March 19, 2011 |newspaper=[[The Press-Enterprise]]}}</ref>
Moon perigee: Unlike most satellites of other planets, the Moon's orbital plane is closer to the [[ecliptic plane]] than to the planet's [[equatorial plane]]. The Moon's orbit is subtly [[perturbation (astronomy)|perturbed]] by the Sun and Earth in many small, complex and interacting ways. For example, the plane of the Moon's orbit [[lunar standstill|gradually rotates]] once every 18.61{{nbsp}}years,<ref>{{cite journal |author1=Haigh, I. D. |author2=Eliot, M. |author3=Pattiaratchi, C. |year=2011 |title=Global influences of the 18.61 year nodal cycle and 8.85 year cycle of lunar perigee on high tidal levels |journal=J. Geophys. Res. |volume=116 |issue=C6 |pages=C06025 |doi=10.1029/2010JC006645 |bibcode=2011JGRC..116.6025H |url=https://api.research-repository.uwa.edu.au/files/3380567/A0059.pdf |access-date=September 24, 2019 |archive-date=December 12, 2019 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20191212170314/https://api.research-repository.uwa.edu.au/files/3380567/A0059.pdf |url-status=live |doi-access=free}}</ref> which affects other aspects of lunar motion. These follow-on effects are mathematically described by [[Cassini's laws]].<ref name="Beletskii2" />
Moon perigee: On average the Moon's [[angular diameter]] is about 0.52°, roughly the same apparent size as the Sun (see {{section link||Eclipses}}). Its apparent size and brightness vary due to its elliptical orbit, appearing up to 30% brighter and 14% larger at perigee compared to apogee, a phenomenon known as a "[[Supermoon]]". In addition, a purely psychological effect, known as the [[Moon illusion]], makes the Moon appear larger when close to the horizon.<ref>{{cite book |last=Hershenson |first=Maurice |title=The Moon illusion |date=1989 |publisher=[[Routledge]] |isbn=978-0-8058-0121-7 |page=5}}</ref>
Moon perigee: In Earth's sky brightness and apparent size of the Moon changes also due to its elliptic [[Orbit of the Moon|orbit around Earth]]. At [[perigee]] (closest), since the Moon is up to 14% closer to Earth than at [[apogee]] (most distant), it subtends a [[solid angle]] which is up to 30% larger. Consequently, given the same phase, the Moon's brightness also varies by up to 30% between apogee and perigee.<ref>{{cite web |url=http://www.space.com/34515-supermoon-guide.html |title=Supermoon November 2016 |date=November 13, 2016 |access-date=November 14, 2016 |publisher=Space.com |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20161114220725/http://www.space.com/34515-supermoon-guide.html |archive-date=November 14, 2016}}</ref> A full (or new) moon at such a position is called a [[supermoon]].<ref name="size1" /><ref name="size2" /><ref>{{cite news |url=https://www.theguardian.com/science/2011/mar/19/super-moon-closest-point-years |title='Super moon' to reach closest point for almost 20 years |newspaper=The Guardian |date=March 19, 2011 |access-date=March 19, 2011 |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20131225175506/http://www.theguardian.com/science/2011/mar/19/super-moon-closest-point-years |archive-date=December 25, 2013}}</ref>
Moon perigee: Each of the four intermediate phases of the Moon lasts, on average, about seven days (approximately 7.38 days), but this duration can vary by about ±11% due to the change in the distance between the Moon and Earth between apogee (farthest point) and perigee (closest point).
Moon perigee: Because the distance between the Moon and Earth is very slowly increasing over time,<ref name="Lambeck1977" /> the angular diameter of the Moon is decreasing. As it evolves toward becoming a [[red giant]], the size of the Sun, and its apparent diameter in the sky, are slowly increasing.{{efn|name=size changes}} The combination of these two changes means that hundreds of millions of years ago, the Moon would always completely cover the Sun on solar eclipses, and no annular eclipses were possible. Likewise, hundreds of millions of years in the future, the Moon will no longer cover the Sun completely, and total solar eclipses will not occur.<ref name=fourmilab>{{cite web |last=Walker |first=John |url=http://www.fourmilab.ch/images/peri_apo/ |title=Moon near Perigee, Earth near Aphelion |publisher=[[Fourmilab]] |date=July 10, 2004 |access-date=December 25, 2013 |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20131208153430/http://www.fourmilab.ch/images/peri_apo/ |archive-date=December 8, 2013}}</ref>

Kipchoge: '''Eliud Kipchoge''' {{Post-nominals|list=[[Order of the Golden Heart (Kenya)|EGH]]}} (born 5 November 1984) is a Kenyan [[long-distance runner]] who competes in the [[marathon]] and formerly specialized in the [[5000 metres]]. Kipchoge is the [[Athletics at the 2016 Summer Olympics – Men's marathon|2016]] and [[Athletics at the 2020 Summer Olympics – Men's marathon|2020]] Olympic marathon champion, and was the [[marathon world record progression|world record]] holder in the marathon from 2018 to 2023,<ref name="George Ramsay">{{Cite web |author=George Ramsay |title=Eliud Kipchoge is the 'greatest of all time ... in any sport' |date=8 August 2021 |url=https://www.cnn.com/2021/08/08/sport/eliud-kipchoge-olympic-marathon-spt-intl/index.html |access-date=20 March 2022 |publisher=CNN |archive-date=20 April 2023 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20230420060021/https://www.cnn.com/2021/08/08/sport/eliud-kipchoge-olympic-marathon-spt-intl/index.html |url-status=live }}</ref> until that record was broken by [[Kelvin Kiptum]] at the [[2023 Chicago Marathon]]. He is widely considered to be one of the greatest marathon runners of all time.<ref>{{cite web |title=All time Top lists – Marathon Men – Senior {{!}} until 8 October 2023 {{!}} All |url=https://worldathletics.org/records/all-time-toplists/road-running/marathon/outdoor/men/senior?regionType=world&drop=regular&fiftyPercentRule=regular&page=1&bestResultsOnly=false&firstDay=1899-12-30&lastDay=2023-10-08 |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20231010173029/https://worldathletics.org/records/all-time-toplists/road-running/marathon/outdoor/men/senior?regionType=world&drop=regular&fiftyPercentRule=regular&page=1&bestResultsOnly=false&firstDay=1899-12-28&lastDay=2023-10-08 |archive-date=10 October 2023 |access-date=10 October 2023 |website=[[World Athletics]]}}</ref><ref name="George Ramsay"/>
Kipchoge: He switched to [[road running]] in 2012 and made the second-fastest [[half marathon]] debut ever, at 59:25. In his marathon debut, he won the 2013 [[Hamburg Marathon]] in a course record time. His first victory at a [[World Marathon Major]] came at the [[Chicago Marathon]] in 2014, and he went on to become series champion a record five times – for 2016, 2017, 2018, 2019 and 2022. He has won the [[London Marathon]] a record four times and also holds the record for most [[Berlin Marathon]] wins with five, his latest coming in September 2023. With 15 victories in his first 18 marathons from 2013 to 2023, Kipchoge's only losses were a second-place finish behind [[Wilson Kipsang Kiprotich]] at the [[2013 Berlin Marathon]], where Kipsang broke the world record, an eighth-place finish at the [[2020 London Marathon]] and a sixth place in his debut at the [[Boston Marathon]] in [[2023 Boston Marathon|2023]].<ref name="News">{{Cite web |url=https://www.leichtathletik.de/news/news/detail/20237-stunden-eliud-kipchoge-bestaetigt-in-london-seine-vormachtstellung/ |title=News |date=28 April 2019 |website=leichtathletik.de |language=de |access-date=28 April 2019 |archive-date=28 April 2019 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20190428134916/https://www.leichtathletik.de/news/news/detail/20237-stunden-eliud-kipchoge-bestaetigt-in-london-seine-vormachtstellung/ |url-status=live }}</ref><ref name="BBC Sport">{{Cite news |url=https://www.bbc.com/sport/athletics/24322574 |title=Berlin marathon: Wilson Kipsang sets new world record |date=29 September 2013 |work=BBC Sport |access-date=1 October 2018 |archive-date=1 October 2018 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20181001182250/https://www.bbc.com/sport/athletics/24322574 |url-status=live }}</ref><ref name="runningmagazine.ca">{{cite web |last1=Snider-McGrath |first1=Ben |title=Shura Kitata wins London Marathon in sprint finish, Kipchoge 8th |url=https://runningmagazine.ca/sections/runs-races/shura-kitata-wins-london-marathon-in-sprint-finish-kipchoge-8th/ |website=Canadian Running Magazine |date=4 October 2020 |access-date=5 October 2020 |archive-date=24 November 2020 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20201124032136/https://runningmagazine.ca/sections/runs-races/shura-kitata-wins-london-marathon-in-sprint-finish-kipchoge-8th/ |url-status=live }}</ref> He has since 2024, been defeated in his last three marathons. Kipchoge's last world record run broke by 30 seconds his own 2018 world record, which was in turn a 78-second improvement over the existing best, the greatest improvement in a marathon world record time since 1967.

Kipchoge: He made his [[half marathon]] debut in the [[Lille Half Marathon]].<ref>{{cite news |url=http://www.iaaf.org/news/news/chebii-clocks-5905-course-record-in-lille-hal |title=Chebii clocks 59:05 course record in Lille Half Marathon |last1=Ramsak |first1=Bob |date=2 September 2012 |access-date=19 January 2013 |publisher=IAAF |last2=Juck |first2=Alfons |archive-date=11 February 2013 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20130211195412/http://www.iaaf.org/news/news/chebii-clocks-5905-course-record-in-lille-hal |url-status=live }}</ref> The run was won by a new course record time of 59:05 (previously 59:36 by ilahun Regassa set in 2008) by Ezekiel Chebii (former personal_best 59:22), trailed by Bernard Koech 59:10, and Kipchoge earned a third place with 59:25. His time of 59:25 became the second fastest Half Marathon debut, only second to Moses Mosop's 59:20 in Milan in 2010.<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://www.iaaf.org/news/news/chebii-clocks-5905-course-record-in-lille-hal|title=IAAF: Chebii clocks 59:05 course record in Lille Half Marathon{{!}} News {{!}} iaaf.org|website=iaaf.org|access-date=28 September 2018|archive-date=17 September 2018|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20180917225227/https://www.iaaf.org/news/news/chebii-clocks-5905-course-record-in-lille-hal|url-status=live}}</ref>

Kipchoge: On 2 February, Kipchoge participated in the Ras al-Khaimah Half Marathon. He placed sixth with a time of 1:00:50. The run was won by Mosinet Geremew (Ethiopia) in 1:00:05.<ref>{{Cite web |url=https://www.letsrun.com/news/2015/02/2015-rak-half-marathon-recap-marvelous-mary-keitany-remember-drone/ |title=2015 RAK Half Marathon Recap: Marvelous Mary Keitany And Remember The Drone |date=13 February 2015 |website=LetsRun.com |access-date=14 October 2019 |archive-date=14 October 2019 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20191014094917/https://www.letsrun.com/news/2015/02/2015-rak-half-marathon-recap-marvelous-mary-keitany-remember-drone/ |url-status=live }}</ref> Kipchoge ran 2:04:42 to win the [[2015 London Marathon]] in April. He also won the [[2015 Berlin Marathon]] later in the year. His win and then-personal best time (2:04:00) occurred even though his shoes malfunctioned, causing his insoles to flap out of both shoes from 10 km onward; rather than risk time lost from an adjustment, he finished the race with bloodied, blistered feet.<ref>{{cite magazine |url=https://www.runnersworld.com/news/a20853873/kipchoge-wins-berlin-marathon-despite-shoe-malfunction/ |first=Cathal |last=Dennehy |title=Despite Insoles Coming Loose, Eliud Kipchoge Wins Berlin Marathon |date=27 September 2015 |access-date=30 September 2018 |magazine=Runner's World |archive-date=30 September 2018 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20180930054148/https://www.runnersworld.com/news/a20853873/kipchoge-wins-berlin-marathon-despite-shoe-malfunction/ |url-status=live }}</ref>
Kipchoge: In April, Kipchoge won the [[2016 London Marathon]] for the second consecutive year in a time of 2:03:05.<ref>{{Cite web |url=https://bleacherreport.com/articles/2635264-london-marathon-2016-results-men-and-womens-top-finishers |title=Retrieved 22 May 2016. |website=[[Bleacher Report]] |access-date=22 May 2016 |archive-date=5 June 2016 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20160605011107/http://bleacherreport.com/articles/2635264-london-marathon-2016-results-men-and-womens-top-finishers |url-status=live }}</ref> His performance broke the course record in London and became the second-fastest marathon time in history, missing [[Dennis Kimetto]]'s world record by 8 seconds.<ref>{{Cite web |url=https://www.iaaf.org/records/all-time-toplists/road-running/marathon/outdoor/men/senior?regionType=world&drop=regular&fiftyPercentRule=regular&page=1&bestResultsOnly=true&firstDay=1899-12-31&lastDay=2016-04-24 |title=Retrieved 20 September 2018. |access-date=20 September 2018 |archive-date=20 September 2018 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20180920122639/https://www.iaaf.org/records/all-time-toplists/road-running/marathon/outdoor/men/senior?regionType=world&drop=regular&fiftyPercentRule=regular&page=1&bestResultsOnly=true&firstDay=1899-12-31&lastDay=2016-04-24 |url-status=live }}</ref>
Kipchoge: As the prerace favourite, during the [[Athletics at the 2016 Summer Olympics|2016 Rio Summer Olympics]], Kipchoge gained a gold medal in the [[athletics at the 2016 Summer Olympics|marathon]] event.<ref>{{Cite news |url=https://www.runnersworld.com/news/a20818616/mens-marathon-eliud-kipchoge-wins-galen-rupp-gets-bronze/ |title=Men's Marathon: Eliud Kipchoge Wins, Galen Rupp Gets Bronze |date=21 August 2016 |work=Runner's World |access-date=4 October 2018 |language=en-US |archive-date=4 October 2018 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20181004230031/https://www.runnersworld.com/news/a20818616/mens-marathon-eliud-kipchoge-wins-galen-rupp-gets-bronze/ |url-status=live }}</ref><ref>{{Cite news |url=https://www.bbc.com/sport/olympics/36727865 |title=Rio Olympics 2016: Kenya's Eliud Kipchoge wins men's marathon |date=21 August 2016 |work=BBC Sport |access-date=26 September 2018 |language=en-GB |archive-date=26 September 2018 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20180926212641/https://www.bbc.com/sport/olympics/36727865 |url-status=live }}</ref><ref>{{Cite web |url=http://www.latimes.com/sports/olympics/la-sp-oly-rio-2016-kipchoge-of-kenya-wins-men-s-marathon-1471791537-htmlstory.html |title=Rio Olympics: Eliud Kipchoge of Kenya wins men's marathon; Galen Rupp of the U.S. takes bronze |last=Dillman |first=Lisa |website=[[Los Angeles Times]] |date=27 August 2016 |access-date=26 September 2018 |archive-date=26 September 2018 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20180926205804/http://www.latimes.com/sports/olympics/la-sp-oly-rio-2016-kipchoge-of-kenya-wins-men-s-marathon-1471791537-htmlstory.html |url-status=live }}</ref> On the last day of the Olympic Games on 21 August 2016, he won in a time of 2:08:44. The runner up was Feyisa Lilesa (Ethiopia) in 2:09:54 and the bronze medal went to Galen Rupp (USA), doing his second marathon, crossing the finish line in 2:10:05. When the halfway point after 21.0975 km was reached, 37 men were within 10 seconds of the lead runner. The participants' field diminished to 3 lead runners shortly before 34 km. Kipchoge made his final move on silver medal winner Lilesa around 36 km into the race. He covered the first half of the race in 1:05:55 while doing the second half in 1:02:49, which amounts to a difference of more than 3 minutes, a negative split.<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://www.iaaf.org/news/report/rio-2016-men-marathon|title=IAAF: Report: men's marathon – Rio 2016 Olympic Games{{!}} News {{!}} iaaf.org|website=iaaf.org|access-date=29 September 2018|archive-date=16 September 2018|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20180916160144/https://www.iaaf.org/news/report/rio-2016-men-marathon|url-status=live}}</ref><ref name="Ingle">{{Cite web |url=https://www.theguardian.com/sport/2016/aug/21/eliud-kipchoge-callum-hawkins-feyisa-lilesa-olympic-marathon |title=Eliud Kipchoge powers to marathon gold as Callum Hawkins finishes ninth |last=Ingle |first=Sean |date=21 August 2016 |website=The Guardian |language=en |access-date=28 September 2018 |archive-date=21 August 2016 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20160821222328/https://www.theguardian.com/sport/2016/aug/21/eliud-kipchoge-callum-hawkins-feyisa-lilesa-olympic-marathon |url-status=live }}</ref> The winning gap between Kipchoge and Lilesa by 70 seconds was the largest victory margin since the [[Athletics at the 1972 Summer Olympics – Men's marathon|1972 Olympic marathon]].<ref>{{Cite news |url=https://www.flotrack.org/articles/5054839-eliud-kipchoge-wins-olympic-marathon-galen-rupp-takes-bronze |title=Eliud Kipchoge Wins Olympic Marathon, Galen Rupp Takes Bronze |access-date=28 September 2018 |language=en-US |archive-date=29 September 2018 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20180929000314/https://www.flotrack.org/articles/5054839-eliud-kipchoge-wins-olympic-marathon-galen-rupp-takes-bronze |url-status=live }}</ref> Kipchoge's winning time of 2:08:44 was, as of August 2021, his slowest marathon time. One hundred fifty-five runners started the race, the largest field in Olympic history; 140 of them finished the race.<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://www.iaaf.org/competitions/olympic-games/the-xxxi-olympic-games-5771/results/men/marathon/final/result|title=IAAF: Marathon Result {{!}} The XXXI Olympic Games {{!}} iaaf.org|website=iaaf.org|access-date=29 September 2018|archive-date=29 September 2018|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20180929233451/https://www.iaaf.org/competitions/olympic-games/the-xxxi-olympic-games-5771/results/men/marathon/final/result|url-status=live}}</ref><ref>{{Cite news |url=http://www.espn.com/espnw/sports/article/17359189/eliud-kipchoge-kenya-wins-olympic-men-marathon-american-galen-rupp-takes-bronze |title=Eliud Kipchoge of Kenya wins Olympic men's marathon; American Galen Rupp takes bronze |work=espnW |access-date=28 September 2018 |archive-date=29 September 2018 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20180929000531/http://www.espn.com/espnw/sports/article/17359189/eliud-kipchoge-kenya-wins-olympic-men-marathon-american-galen-rupp-takes-bronze |url-status=live }}</ref> With this win, Kipchoge became the second Kenyan male after Sammy Wanjiru in [[Athletics at the 2008 Summer Olympics|Beijing 2008]] to win an Olympic marathon gold medal. At the same Olympics, the women's marathon was won by [[Jemima Sumgong]], who became the first female Kenyan winner.<ref>{{Cite web |url=https://www.theguardian.com/sport/2016/aug/14/jemima-sumgong-wins-olympic-marathon-gold-kenya |title=Jemima Sumgong wins Olympic marathon gold for Kenya |author=<!--not stated--> |agency=Reuters |date=14 August 2016 |website=The Guardian |language=en |access-date=1 October 2018 |archive-date=2 October 2018 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20181002020158/https://www.theguardian.com/sport/2016/aug/14/jemima-sumgong-wins-olympic-marathon-gold-kenya |url-status=live }}</ref><ref name="Ingle" />
Kipchoge: On 6 May, Kipchoge, along with Zersenay Tadese (then world record holder in the half marathon) and [[Lelisa Desisa]] (2-time Boston Marathon winner), attempted the first sub-two-hour assisted marathon in the Nike [[Breaking2]] project on the [[Monza]] [[Autodromo Nazionale Monza|Formula 1 racetrack]] near [[Milan]], Italy. All three runners ran a test 2 months before the attempt. The target time was 1 hour for a half Marathon. Kipchoge finished first in 59:17. The course was measured at 2400 m per lap.<ref>{{Cite web |url=https://www.runnersworld.com/news/a20849569/sub-2-marathon-test-run-yields-fast-times-lingering-questions/ |title=Sub-2 Marathon Test Run Yields Fast Times, Lingering Questions |last=Hutchinson |first=Alex |date=7 March 2017 |website=Runner's World |language=en-US |access-date=10 May 2019 |archive-date=10 May 2019 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20190510141834/https://www.runnersworld.com/news/a20849569/sub-2-marathon-test-run-yields-fast-times-lingering-questions/ |url-status=live }}</ref> During the 2-hour attempt, the runners were paced by a lead car and 30 supporting pacers joining in stages (both considered illegal under [[IAAF]] rules).<ref name="veconomist">{{cite news |author=J.S. |title=Can the marathon's two-hour barrier be broken? |url=https://www.economist.com/blogs/gametheory/2017/10/runnin-down-dream |newspaper=[[The Economist]] |date=4 October 2017 |access-date=4 October 2017 |archive-date=15 May 2018 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20180515095632/https://www.economist.com/blogs/gametheory/2017/10/runnin-down-dream |url-status=live }}</ref> The race started at 5:45h local time on the 2.4 km track. Kipchoge finished in 2:00:25, while the other two had to slow and finished far behind.<ref>{{Cite web |url=http://www.herbertsteffny.de/artikel/Nike_Sub_2Hours.htm |title=Sub 2:00 Hours Marathon – kritisch hinterfragt |website=herbertsteffny.de |language=de-de |access-date=29 September 2018 |archive-date=13 October 2018 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20181013041808/http://www.herbertsteffny.de/artikel/Nike_Sub_2Hours.htm |url-status=live }}</ref> The runners planned even 14:13 5k splits to break 2 hours. His 5k splits were: 14:14, 14:07, 14:13, 14:15, 14:14, 14:17, 14:17, 14:27, and 6:20 to finish.<ref>{{Cite news |url=https://www.theguardian.com/sport/live/2017/may/06/sub-two-hour-marathon-attempt-in-monza-live |title=Eliud Kipchoge misses sub two-hour marathon target in Monza – as it happened |last=Caroll |first=James |date=6 May 2017 |work=The Guardian |access-date=30 April 2018 |language=en-GB |issn=0261-3077 |archive-date=22 April 2018 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20180422224117/https://www.theguardian.com/sport/live/2017/may/06/sub-two-hour-marathon-attempt-in-monza-live |url-status=live }}</ref> The 5k split times from 25k and further would be world records: 25k in 1:11:03, 30k in 1:25:20, 35k in 1:39:37, 40k in 1:54:04.

Kipchoge: On 16 September, Kipchoge won the [[2018 Berlin Marathon]] in a time of 2:01:39, breaking the previous world record by 1 minute and 18 seconds (2:02:57 set by fellow countryman Dennis Kimetto at the Berlin Marathon in 2014). It was the greatest improvement in a marathon world record time since 1967.<ref>{{cite web |last1=Robinson |first1=Roger |title=Eliud Kipchoge Crushes Marathon World Record at Berlin Marathon |date=16 September 2018 |url=https://www.runnersworld.com/news/a23244541/berlin-marathon-world-record/ |publisher=Runner's World |access-date=21 October 2019 |archive-date=31 August 2019 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20190831110153/https://www.runnersworld.com/news/a23244541/berlin-marathon-world-record/ |url-status=live }}</ref> He finished 4:43 min ahead of second-placed fellow Kenyan Amos Kipruto. The world record holder from 2013, Wilson Kipsang of Kenya, came in third at 2:06:48.<ref>{{Cite news |url=https://www.welt.de/sport/article181548434/Berlin-Marathon-2018-Kenianer-Eliud-Kipchoge-knackt-den-Weltrekord.html |title=Berlin-Marathon 2018: Kenianer Eliud Kipchoge knackt den Weltrekord |last=WELT |date=16 September 2018 |work=DIE WELT |language=de |access-date=16 September 2018 |archive-date=19 September 2018 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20180919100330/https://www.welt.de/sport/article181548434/Berlin-Marathon-2018-Kenianer-Eliud-Kipchoge-knackt-den-Weltrekord.html |url-status=live }}</ref><ref>{{Cite web|url=https://www.iaaf.org/news/report/wilson-kipsang-sets-world-record-of-20323-in|title=IAAF: Kipsang sets world record of 2:03:23 at Berlin Marathon|website=iaaf.org|access-date=17 September 2018|archive-date=26 March 2018|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20180326142253/https://www.iaaf.org/news/report/wilson-kipsang-sets-world-record-of-20323-in|url-status=live}}</ref> It was the 11th world record set at the Berlin Marathon.<ref name="BerlinRecords" />

|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20210509052811/https://www.guinnessworldrecords.com/world-records/595080-first-marathon-distance-under-two-hours |url-status=live }}</ref>
Kipchoge: Kipchoge placed 8th in the [[2020 London Marathon]] in October with a time of 2:06:49, the lowest finish of his marathoning career so far.<ref name="runningmagazine.ca"/> The race was won by Ehtopias'S Shura Itata in a time of 2:05:41. Kipchoge lost contact with the lead runner with 3 miles to go. For the first time, the run was on a 19 laps looped course and originally set for April and postponed to October due to the Covid 19 pandemic.[https://worldathletics.org/news/report/london-marathon-2020-kitata-kosgei-kipchoge]
Kipchoge: In preparation for the delayed [[Athletics at the 2020 Summer Olympics|2020 Tokyo Olympic Games]], he won the ''NN Mission Marathon'', which was held at [[Enschede Airport Twente]] in the Netherlands on 18 April 2021 in a time of 2:04:30. Jonathan Korir finished as the runner up with a personal best of 2:06:40.<ref>{{Cite web|date=18 April 2021|title=Athletics news – Rejuvenated Eliud Kipchoge wins NN Mission Marathon in Enschede, Netherlands|url=https://www.eurosport.com/athletics/tokyo-2020/2021/athletics-news-rejuvenated-eliud-kipchoge-wins-nn-mission-marathon-in-enschede-the-netherlands_sto8276988/story.shtml|access-date=18 April 2021|website=Eurosport|language=en|archive-date=20 April 2023|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20230420060020/https://www.eurosport.com/geoblocking.shtml|url-status=live}}</ref>
Kipchoge: Kipchoge successfully defended his title from the Rio Olympics by winning the gold medal in the men's marathon at the Tokyo Games in a time of 2:08:38, becoming only the third person to successfully defend their gold medal in the men's marathon, after [[Abebe Bikila]] in 1960 and 1964, and [[Waldemar Cierpinski]] in 1976 and 1980.<ref>{{Cite news|last=Longman|first=Jeré|date=8 August 2021|title=Kipchoge finished far ahead of the pack to defend his men's Olympic marathon title.|language=en-US|work=The New York Times|url=https://www.nytimes.com/2021/08/07/sports/olympics/marathon-results-kipchoge-galen-rupp.html|access-date=8 August 2021|issn=0362-4331|archive-date=8 August 2021|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20210808010742/https://www.nytimes.com/2021/08/07/sports/olympics/marathon-results-kipchoge-galen-rupp.html|url-status=live}}</ref> He was the favourite to win and attacked around the 30 km mark, looking back only once afterwards. He won by 80 seconds, the largest margin in 49 years.<ref>{{Cite web |last= |date=12 January 2022 |title=2021 LetsRun Awards |url=https://www.letsrun.com/news/2022/01/2021-letsrun-awards-best-athlete-best-comeback-best-wtf-performance-biggest-heartbreak-more/ |access-date=3 January 2023 |website=[[LetsRun.com]] |language=en |archive-date=3 January 2023 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20230103132745/https://www.letsrun.com/news/2022/01/2021-letsrun-awards-best-athlete-best-comeback-best-wtf-performance-biggest-heartbreak-more/ |url-status=live }}</ref> The silver medal went to [[Abdi Nageeye]] (Netherlands), while [[Bashir Abdi]] (Belgium) came in third for a bronze medal with 2:10:00. Kipchoge was the oldest Olympic marathon winner since [[Carlos Lopes]] won in 1984 at the age of 37. The run was staged 500 miles north of Tokyo in [[Sapporo]], with 106 runners participating.<ref>{{Cite web|title=Kenya's Eliud Kipchoge repeats as Olympic marathon champion|url=https://abcnews.go.com/Sports/kenyas-eliud-kipchoge-repeats-olympic-marathon-champion/story?id=79343991|access-date=8 August 2021|website=ABC News|language=en|archive-date=8 August 2021|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20210808155313/https://abcnews.go.com/Sports/kenyas-eliud-kipchoge-repeats-olympic-marathon-champion/story?id=79343991|url-status=live}}</ref> A documentary on the Ineos 1:59 Challenge, titled ''[[Kipchoge: The Last Milestone]]'', was released digitally [[video on demand|on-demand]] on 24 August 2021.
Kipchoge: On 20 January, Kipchoge announced his desire to win all six [[World Marathon Majors]] (he had already won three, the London, Berlin, and Chicago marathons by that time). This was followed up by an announcement on 18 February that he would be participating in the [[2021 Tokyo Marathon]] (which took place on 6 March 2022 due to [[COVID-19]] restrictions in 2021) and that the majority of his recent training has been dedicated towards this goal.<ref>{{Cite news|title=Olympic champion Kipchoge to participate in Tokyo Marathon|url=https://www.reuters.com/lifestyle/sports/olympic-champion-kipchoge-participate-tokyo-marathon-2022-02-18/|access-date=18 February 2022|publisher=Reuters|date=18 February 2022|language=en|archive-date=18 February 2022|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20220218134350/https://www.reuters.com/lifestyle/sports/olympic-champion-kipchoge-participate-tokyo-marathon-2022-02-18/|url-status=live}}</ref> He won the Tokyo Marathon with a time of 2:02:40 – a course and all-comers' record. [[Amos Kipruto]] of Kenya finished second with a personal best of 2:03:13, and [[Tamirat Tola]] from Ethiopia came in third in a time of 2:04:14.<ref>{{Cite web |title=Kipchoge and Kosgei race to Japanese all-comers' records in Tokyo |url=https://worldathletics.org/competitions/world-athletics-label-road-races/news/kipchoge-kosgei-all-comers-records-tokyo-marathon |access-date=6 March 2022 |website=[[World Athletics]] |archive-date=6 March 2022 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20220306050741/https://www.worldathletics.org/competitions/world-athletics-label-road-races/news/kipchoge-kosgei-all-comers-records-tokyo-marathon |url-status=live }}</ref>
Kipchoge: ====2022 Berlin and second world marathon record====
Kipchoge: On 25 September, Kipchoge won the [[2022 Berlin Marathon|Berlin Marathon]] decisively in a time of 2:01:09, beating by 30 seconds his own previous world record, which he set on the same course in 2018. With his fourth victory in Berlin, he equalled the record achievement of [[Haile Gebrselassie]]. He finished 4:49 min ahead of second-placed compatriot [[Mark Korir]] while Ethiopia's Tadu Abate took third place with a time of 2:06:28. Kipchoge achieved halfway in 59:51 which, being at the time, the fastest split in marathon history, would have been a world record in the standalone half-marathon in 1993, and was only 26 seconds off his best in that distance. He slowed down later with second half in 61:18.<ref>{{Cite web |url=https://www.bbc.com/sport/athletics/63025365 |language=en-GB |date=25 September 2022 |access-date=25 September 2022 |title=Eliud Kipchoge breaks his own marathon world record in Berlin |publisher=[[BBC News]] |archive-date=25 September 2022 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20220925093052/https://www.bbc.com/sport/athletics/63025365 |url-status=live }}</ref><ref>{{Cite web |date=25 September 2022 |title=Kipchoge breaks world record in Berlin with 2:01:09 |url=https://worldathletics.org/news/report/eliud-kipchoge-world-record-berlin-marathon-2022 |access-date=25 September 2022 |website=[[World Athletics]] |archive-date=25 September 2022 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20220925100720/https://www.worldathletics.org/news/report/eliud-kipchoge-world-record-berlin-marathon-2022 |url-status=live }}</ref><ref>{{Cite web |date=25 September 2022 |title=Eliud Kipchoge (2:01:09) Smashes World Record; Tigist Assefa (2:15:37) Stuns World at 2022 Berlin Marathon |url=https://www.letsrun.com/news/2022/09/eliud-kipchoge-20109-smashes-world-record-tigist-assefa-21537-stuns-world-at-2022-berlin-marathon/ |access-date=25 September 2022 |website=[[LetsRun.com]] |language=en |archive-date=25 September 2022 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20220925095052/https://www.letsrun.com/news/2022/09/eliud-kipchoge-20109-smashes-world-record-tigist-assefa-21537-stuns-world-at-2022-berlin-marathon/ |url-status=live }}</ref><ref>{{Cite web |last=Henderson |first=Jason |date=25 September 2022 |title=Eliud Kipchoge smashes world marathon record in Berlin |url=https://athleticsweekly.com/event-reports/eliud-kipchoge-smashes-world-marathon-record-in-berlin-1039961124/ |access-date=25 September 2022 |website=[[Athletics Weekly|AW]] |language=en-GB |archive-date=25 September 2022 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20220925105142/https://athleticsweekly.com/event-reports/eliud-kipchoge-smashes-world-marathon-record-in-berlin-1039961124/ |url-status=live }}</ref> It was the eighth time in a row that men's record was set in Berlin and 12th record there overall.<ref>{{Cite news |last=Schmitz |first=Rob |date=25 September 2022 |title=He was so fast, he had time to celebrate long before the second-place runner arrived |language=en |publisher=[[NPR]] |url=https://www.npr.org/2022/09/25/1124986817/eliud-kipchoge-world-record-berlin-marathon |access-date=27 September 2022 |archive-date=26 September 2022 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20220926212453/https://www.npr.org/2022/09/25/1124986817/eliud-kipchoge-world-record-berlin-marathon |url-status=live }}</ref><ref name="BerlinRecords" />

Kipchoge: At the [[2023 Boston Marathon]], Kipchoge aimed to win his fifth of the six major marathons. However, after missing his water bottle and due to a left leg problem,<ref>{{Cite web |last=Lorge Butler |first=Sarah |date=18 April 2023 |title=Eliud Kipchoge Says Left Leg Pain Plagued Him During Boston Marathon |url=https://www.runnersworld.com/news/a43633747/eliud-kipchoge-leg-pain-boston-marathon-2023/ |access-date=18 April 2023 |website=[[Runner's World]] |archive-date=20 April 2023 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20230420060020/https://www.runnersworld.com/news/a43633747/eliud-kipchoge-leg-pain-boston-marathon-2023/ |url-status=live }}</ref><ref>{{Cite web |last=Cacciola |first=Scott |date=18 April 2023 |title=Eliud Kipchoge Was Supposed to Win the Boston Marathon. What Went Wrong? |url=https://www.nytimes.com/2023/04/18/sports/eliud-kipchoge-boston-marathon.html |access-date=18 April 2023 |website=[[The New York Times]] |issn=0362-4331 |archive-date=19 April 2023 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20230419010256/https://www.nytimes.com/2023/04/18/sports/eliud-kipchoge-boston-marathon.html/ |url-status=live }}</ref> the 38-year-old was unable to stay with the lead group on a hilly section after the 30 km mark. He suffered the third defeat of his marathon career, finishing sixth with a time of 2:09:23. [[Evans Chebet]] was the winner in 2:05:54, successfully defending his title.<ref>{{Cite web |date=17 April 2023 |title=Chebet retains Boston title while Obiri claims first major marathon victory |url=https://worldathletics.org/news/report/boston-marathon-2023-obiri-chebet |access-date=17 April 2023 |website=[[World Athletics]] |archive-date=20 April 2023 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20230420060024/https://worldathletics.org/news/report/boston-marathon-2023-obiri-chebet |url-status=live }}</ref>
Kipchoge: At the [[2023 Berlin Marathon]], his first race since the Boston defeat, Kipchoge won the race for a record fifth time, finishing at 2:02:42. He ran alone from {{convert|32|km|abbr=on}} onward after Ethiopia's Derseh Kindie dropped away, but fell short of breaking his own world record that he had set the previous year. With the victory, Kipchoge became the first man in history to win the Berlin Marathon five times, having already won in 2015, 2017, 2018, and 2022.{{citation needed|date=October 2025}} Fellow Kenyan Vincent Kipkemoi came in third place in a time of 2:03:13. The half marathon split time was 1:00:22.[https://worldathletics.org/news/report/tigst-assefa-world-marathon-record-berlin-kipchoge-2023]
Kipchoge: The Marathons winner was Tamirat Tola (Ethopia) in a time of 2:06:26 an Olympic record, silver went to Bashir Abdi (Belgium) 2:06:47 and bronze to Benson Kipruto (Kenay) 2:07:00. Kipchoge's longtime rival Kenenisa Bekele finished2:12:24 placed 39 among 71 finishers with 10 runners dit not finish.[https://marathonhandbook.com/kenenisa-bekele-joins-eliud-kipchoge-nyc-marathon/][https://www.watchathletics.com/page/5867/men-s-marathon-results-paris-olympic-games-2024-athletics] Despite the performance, Kenyan President [[William Ruto]] still recognized Kipchoge's achievements: {{blockquote|"I know how people were disappointed. Many people I know made a lot of comments, 'How could Eliud not finish?' But Eliud we celebrate you. You have held our flag high."<ref>{{cite web |archiveurl=https://web.archive.org/web/20240912154257/https://classic105.com/latest/2024-08-15-president-rutos-message-to-eliud-kipchoge-after-olympics-misfortune/ |archivedate=2024-09-12 |title=President Ruto's message to Eliud Kipchoge after Olympic's misfortune |url=https://classic105.com/latest/2024-08-15-president-rutos-message-to-eliud-kipchoge-after-olympics-misfortune/ |date=2024-08-15 |work=Nairobi Classic 105 |quote=Kipchoge's quest in the games came to an abrupt end at the 30km mark due to a sharp pain in his waist. }}</ref>}}

The Moon's orbit is slightly elliptical, with an [[orbital eccentricity]] of 0.055. The [[semi-major axis]] of the geocentric lunar orbit, called the [[lunar distance]], is approximately {{cvt|385,000|km|mi}}, or 1.3 [[light-second]]s, comparable to going [[circumference of Earth|around Earth]] approximately 9.6 times.{{efn |name=distance ratio}}<ref name="allen">{{cite book |last1=Allen |first1=C. W. |title=Allen's Astrophysical Quantities |date=2002 |publisher=Springer |location=New York |isbn=978-1-4612-1186-0 |edition=4th|pages=240,308}}</ref> The distance between the Moon and Earth varies from around {{convert|356,400|km|mi|abbr=on}} ([[perigee]]) to {{convert|406,700|km|mi|abbr=on}} (apogee), making the Moon's distance and apparent size fluctuate up to 14%.<ref name="size1">{{cite web |author=Phillips |first=Tony |date=March 16, 2011 |title=Super Full Moon |url=https://science.nasa.gov/science-news/science-at-nasa/2011/16mar_supermoon/ |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20120507035348/https://science.nasa.gov/science-news/science-at-nasa/2011/16mar_supermoon/ |archive-date=May 7, 2012 |access-date=March 19, 2011 |publisher=NASA}}</ref><ref name="size2">{{cite news |author=De Atley |first=Richard K. |date=March 18, 2011 |title=Full moon tonight is as close as it gets |url=http://www.pe.com/localnews/stories/PE_News_Local_D_moon19.23a6364.html |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20110322161600/http://www.pe.com/localnews/stories/PE_News_Local_D_moon19.23a6364.html |archive-date=March 22, 2011 |access-date=March 19, 2011 |newspaper=[[The Press-Enterprise]]}}</ref>
Unlike most satellites of other planets, the Moon's orbital plane is closer to the [[ecliptic plane]] than to the planet's [[equatorial plane]]. The Moon's orbit is subtly [[perturbation (astronomy)|perturbed]] by the Sun and Earth in many small, complex and interacting ways. For example, the plane of the Moon's orbit [[lunar standstill|gradually rotates]] once every 18.61{{nbsp}}years,<ref>{{cite journal |author1=Haigh, I. D. |author2=Eliot, M. |author3=Pattiaratchi, C. |year=2011 |title=Global influences of the 18.61 year nodal cycle and 8.85 year cycle of lunar perigee on high tidal levels |journal=J. Geophys. Res. |volume=116 |issue=C6 |pages=C06025 |doi=10.1029/2010JC006645 |bibcode=2011JGRC..116.6025H |url=https://api.research-repository.uwa.edu.au/files/3380567/A0059.pdf |access-date=September 24, 2019 |archive-date=December 12, 2019 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20191212170314/https://api.research-repository.uwa.edu.au/files/3380567/A0059.pdf |url-status=live |doi-access=free}}</ref> which affects other aspects of lunar motion. These follow-on effects are mathematically described by [[Cassini's laws]].<ref name="Beletskii2" />
The gravitational attraction that Earth and the Moon (as well as the Sun) exert on each other manifests in a slightly greater attraction on the sides closest to each other, resulting in [[tidal forces]]. [[Ocean tides]] are the most widely experienced result of this, but tidal forces also considerably affect other mechanics of Earth, as well as the Moon and their system.
On average the Moon's [[angular diameter]] is about 0.52°, roughly the same apparent size as the Sun (see {{section link||Eclipses}}). Its apparent size and brightness vary due to its elliptical orbit, appearing up to 30% brighter and 14% larger at perigee compared to apogee, a phenomenon known as a "[[Supermoon]]". In addition, a purely psychological effect, known as the [[Moon illusion]], makes the Moon appear larger when close to the horizon.<ref>{{cite book |last=Hershenson |first=Maurice |title=The Moon illusion |date=1989 |publisher=[[Routledge]] |isbn=978-0-8058-0121-7 |page=5}}</ref>
In Earth's sky brightness and apparent size of the Moon changes also due to its elliptic [[Orbit of the Moon|orbit around Earth]]. At [[perigee]] (closest), since the Moon is up to 14% closer to Earth than at [[apogee]] (most distant), it subtends a [[solid angle]] which is up to 30% larger. Consequently, given the same phase, the Moon's brightness also varies by up to 30% between apogee and perigee.<ref>{{cite web |url=http://www.space.com/34515-supermoon-guide.html |title=Supermoon November 2016 |date=November 13, 2016 |access-date=November 14, 2016 |publisher=Space.com |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20161114220725/http://www.space.com/34515-supermoon-guide.html |archive-date=November 14, 2016}}</ref> A full (or new) moon at such a position is called a [[supermoon]].<ref name="size1" /><ref name="size2" /><ref>{{cite news |url=https://www.theguardian.com/science/2011/mar/19/super-moon-closest-point-years |title='Super moon' to reach closest point for almost 20 years |newspaper=The Guardian |date=March 19, 2011 |access-date=March 19, 2011 |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20131225175506/http://www.theguardian.com/science/2011/mar/19/super-moon-closest-point-years |archive-date=December 25, 2013}}</ref>
Each of the four intermediate phases of the Moon lasts, on average, about seven days (approximately 7.38 days), but this duration can vary by about ±11% due to the change in the distance between the Moon and Earth between apogee (farthest point) and perigee (closest point).
Because the distance between the Moon and Earth is very slowly increasing over time,<ref name="Lambeck1977" /> the angular diameter of the Moon is decreasing. As it evolves toward becoming a [[red giant]], the size of the Sun, and its apparent diameter in the sky, are slowly increasing.{{efn|name=size changes}} The combination of these two changes means that hundreds of millions of years ago, the Moon would always completely cover the Sun on solar eclipses, and no annular eclipses were possible. Likewise, hundreds of millions of years in the future, the Moon will no longer cover the Sun completely, and total solar eclipses will not occur.<ref name=fourmilab>{{cite web |last=Walker |first=John |url=http://www.fourmilab.ch/images/peri_apo/ |title=Moon near Perigee, Earth near Aphelion |publisher=[[Fourmilab]] |date=July 10, 2004 |access-date=December 25, 2013 |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20131208153430/http://www.fourmilab.ch/images/peri_apo/ |archive-date=December 8, 2013}}</ref>
